analytic.title: On the Schedulability Analysis for Distributed Hard Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper we investigate into the validity of the Rate Monotonic Analysis techniques for distributed hard real-time systems. A recent paper has shown that the algorithm developed by Tindell and Clark for the analysis of this kind of system was incomplete because it did not test all the possible cases. We will prove that the algorithm is valid as it is stated and that it effectively obtains an upper bound for the worst-case response times to extemal events in distributed systems, since the longest response always occurs within the cases that are currently tested by this algorithm. In addition, we will extend the analysis technique to determine an upper bound for the local response times of particular actions in a response to an event, thus allowing the definition and verijication of local deadlines for elementary actions in distributed systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The typical architecture in a distributed real-time control system consists of several processor nodes interconnected through one or more interconnection networks. The system's software is composed of concurrent tasks that are often statically allocated to processing nodes, and may exchange messages with other tasks in the same node or in different nodes. Tasks allocated in the same node may also share data or resources via the usual synchronization mechanisms used in shared memory systems. Each task in the system is activated by the arrival of a triggering event that may be generated by the external environment, a timer, or by the arrival of a message from another task. Many of these events have an associated timing requirement, such as an end-to-end deadline, which is the maximum response time allowed from the arrival of an event to its final completion. Other timing requirements may also be imposed on individual actions. This work has been supported in part by the Comisicin Inrevministerial de Cienciu y Tecnologiu of the Spanish Govemment, under Grant In order to make it possible to predict worst-case response times, we can schedule the activities in each processing node using a priority-based approach that allows processing activities with shorter deadlines before (at a higher priority) activities with longer deadlines. One analysis technique used to assess the schedulability of the real-time system is called Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA). This theory has its origins in work carried out by Liu and Layland in 1973 [7] where they introduced Rate Monotonic Scheduling, which is a scheduling algorithm with optimum assignment of static priorities under a particular set of restrictions. Liu and Layland's work was only applicable to extremely restrictive systems and so had limited practical application. However, it served as the basis of many later work in which the imposed restrictions were gradually reduced, until achieving the theoretical body that we now use to analyze hard real-time systems based on fixed priorities [SI.

The RMA techniques can also be applied to distributed systems [8][12] by modeling each network as if it were a processor, and each message as if it were a task. The schedulability analysis techniques developed for distributed real-time systems have permitted the solution to some of the problems involving these systems, such as: the optimization of the scheduling and allocation of tasks to processors and messages to networks [ 111, the optimization of the priority assignment to tasks and messages [l], and the extension of the schedulability analysis techniques to handle complex synchronization patterns among the responses to different event sequences in distributed systems [3][4].

Although the analysis technique developed by Tindell and Clark [12] for obtaining the global response times of tasks and messages in distributed systems has been widely accepted and used, Sun and Liu have shown in a recent paper [9] that its proof is not complete, because it does not test the response times of all the events that may arrive at the system during the interval of time that must be considered for the worst-case analysis, which is called a busy period. They conclude that Tindell and Clark's analysis is incorrect, and propose a new analysis technique that checks all the events that may arrive during the complete busy period. In this paper we will prove that the original analysis technique is valid, because the worst-case response may only occur during the time interval used in Tindell and Clark's equations. This makes the proof of the original analysis technique complete, and thus allows us to continue using it, and to rely on previous analysis results. Moreover, the original analysis technique is faster than the new technique proposed in [9], because the number of events tested is smaller.

Another issue that we address in this paper is the verification of local deadlines associated with a particular action (a task or a message) belonging to a sequence of actions in the response to a particular event. The local deadline is measured relative to the activation of that particular action, as opposed to a global deadline which is measured relative to the arrival of the triggering event. We will show how to obtain an upper bound to the local response time of a particular action, which may then be compared to the associated local deadline. For this case we will see that the analysis interval used in Tindell and Clark's analysis for global response times is not enough, and that we may need to test one more event.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide a quick review of the model that we use for the distributed system and the current analysis technique applicable to this kind of system. Section 3 describes why the proof of Tindell and Clark's analysis technique is not complete, and provides the complete proof. In Section 4 we obtain the worst-case local response times of individual actions in a response to an event sequence, which allow the verification of local deadlines. Finally, in Section 5 we give our conclusions.

div.head: Distributed real-time system model and current analysis technique
div.p: In a distributed system there are several processor resources (CPUs) and one or more communication resources (buses, LANs, serial lines, etc.). We shall assume preemptive scheduling based on fixed priorities, in order to be able to use RMA for the analysis of the worst-case timing behavior of both tasks and messages. We will also assume a real-time communications system that uses priority preemptive scheduling [2], and thus we will treat the messages in the communication resources in the same way as the tasks in the processor resources, except for a small blocking term that must be taken into account because the messages are composed of sequences of packets, each of which is indivisible and non preemptive.

We use the linear model of an event-driven distributed system [3][4], in which there is a set of external event sequences (generated by external devices, timers, etc.) which activate tasks that are distributed in different processors. These tasks may in turn generate internal events which activate other tasks in the same processor, or may activate messages that are sent through a communications network. The arrival of a message at its destination represents an internal event that may activate one or more tasks. We suppose that all the sequences of external events arriving at the system are known in advance, and that the rates at which the events with hard real-time requirements arrive are also known; otherwise, it would be impossible to guarantee the schedulability of the system at compilation time. The internal events are generated by the actions executed as a response to an external event, and therefore, their timing characteristics are derived from it. Furthermore, we suppose that these events are instantaneous and so they will have no influence on the calculation of the worst-case response times of the actions which they activate. This does not mean a loss of generality because the overhead effects of the internal events can be easily included in the analysis as extra execution or transmission time.

Each external event arriving at the system generates a response in the form of a sequence of actions. Each action is activated by the internal events generated by the previous actions. The actions may be tasks (or parts of a task) executed in a particular processor, or messages sent through a communications network. Normally, the first action of a response is a task. We will call e, the external event that activates action a,, and e,k the internal event that activates action a, and was generated by action a,. We will call a job of an action a, each instance of the action execution caused by the arrival of an event. In the linear model of the distributed system, the actions can only be activated from a single event (internal or external), and can only generate one internal event that may in turn activate another single action in the same or in a different resource (processor or network).

There are different kinds of timing requirements that may be imposed on the actions of the response to an external event. We will call global deadline of a particular action the maximum interval of time that may elapse between the arrival of the external event and the finalization of that action, and local deadline of the same action if it is measured relative of the arrival of the internal event. The global deadline of the last action in a response will be called the end-to-end deadline. We will call D, the global deadline of action a,, d, the local deadline of that action, and ED, the end-to-end deadline for action a, (which should be the last action in the response sequence). According to this definition of the linear model for distributed systems, Figure 1 shows the scheme of a linear action that is triggered by an input event and can only generate one output event. The general worst-case analysis of a distributed system that follows the linear model is still an open issue, but one approach that can be used is to analyze each processing and communication resource of the system as if it was independent. The analysis of each resource in the distributed system can be carried out using the normal RMA techniques [6], but taking into account the effects of jitter or deferred activation. In distributed systems the messages are activated by the execution of the tasks, and their activation instants are not perfectly periodic, but depend on the completion time of the triggering task, which is variable. Exactly the same happens with the tasks activated by the arrival of messages.

The solution to this problem was proposed by Tindell and Clark [12] and consists of repeating the worst-case analysis iteratively (calculation of worst-case response times and jitter for all the system's resources) starting with jitter values equal to zero. The monotonic dependency of the response time with respect to jitter makes the analysis converge to a stable solution. As a result of the analysis, the worst-case global responses are obtained and, from them, it can be proved that the schedulability requirements imposed on the distributed system are met. The system is schedulable when the worst-case global response times of each of the actions are less than or equal to their respective deadlines.

div.head: Validity of the current schedulability analysis technique
div.p: An important definition that is used to calculate the worst-case response time of an action a, is the duration of its busy period, which is the maximum interval of time during which the processor is busy executing actions of priority higher than or equal to the priority of a; [6]. Its start coincides with a critical instant for action a, (a worstcase condition at which all higher priority activities are activated simultaneously with a,) and the busy period finalizes when all pending activations of a, have been processed. To create a critical instant, all the initial activations must be delayed as long as possible (by an amount equal to the maximum jitter), and all the following activations must occur at the earliest possible time. div.head: Bounding the worst-case local response times
div.p: In Section 2, we saw that the current analysis techniques for distributed systems are only applicable to determine the worst-case global response times, which are measured relative to the arrival of the triggering event. This Section is devoted to finding an upper bound for the worst-case local response times of an individual action, relative to the activation of that action.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The results presented in this paper consolidate the existing analysis techniques for hard real-time distributed systems based on rate monotonic analysis. We have proved that Tindell and Clark's analysis effectively obtains an upper bound for the worst-case global response times of the tasks or messages in a distributed system. Although the worst-case busy period for a given action includes more jobs than those checked by this analysis technique, the worst case will always occur for the jobs that are checked. Therefore, we can continue using this technique, and the results of previous analysis remain valid.

In addition, we have extended the analysis technique to calculate an upper bound for the worst-case local response times of individual tasks or messages. In this case we have found that it is necessary to analyze one more job of the action (if it belongs to the busy period) in addition to the number of jobs checked with Tindell and Clark's analysis for global response times. With this result it is possible to check whether local deadlines imposed on individual tasks or messages (relative to their own activation) will be met or not.
